# Introduction

Can political bulletins tell us something about party's level of centralization?

# Theory {#sec-theory}

## Literature {#sec-literature}

Why political parties decide to (de)centralize their political
campaign? Arguably, the answer to this question depends on many factor,
and most importantly on the structures under which the elections take
place. Rather than trying to find an answer that would be applicable to
every electoral system, political system, and state's structure (federal
vs. unitary), we will focus on parliamentary single member district
(SMD).  The argument concerns national level elections, therefore it
might not extend to subnational election.

These initial scope conditions are also justified based on the existing 
literature. Previous research have highlighted that as the political and
economic power lies at different levels in federal versus unitary states,
these structures change how party and voters make their strategic choices
[@chhibber_etal04; @mendozagomez26]. 

Why parties (de)centralize campaigns? Some previous explanation focused
on the incentives of candidates to cultivate personal reputation that
is distinct to party reputation [@carey_shugart95]. While this account
situate the candidate as the agent taking the decision, and not about
the party deciding the discretion candidate can have, some elements are
useful to think about this question. Among the most important factors 
is the electoral system, as it shapes the control party leaders have over
the ballot, how pooled the votes are, and how votes are attributed. In 
the case of interest here, in SMD, the personal reputation is least 
important.

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{H1}]: Individual candidates bulletins are aligned with the 
party (little discretionary power).
\end{itemize}
```

However, while being informative about the strategic choices of candidates
in SMD system, this predictions doesn't seem to be adequate. As we'll
present in @sec-context, a key feature of Japanese politics is centered
around personal ties known as Kōenkai. Therefore, it's unrealistic
to expect personal ties to have little to no effect in campaign in
Japan. Account of the historical loss of the LDP in 2009 highlight the
role of party centralization and cut back on particularistic spending
which was the core of the clientelistic foundation of the LPD electoral
dominance [@reed_etal12; @scheiner06]. While @reed_etal12 predicts that 
the shift toward a less discretionary and more nationalized LPD would lead
to the end of single-party dominance in Japan post 2009, this prediction
has yet to be realized. They further add that the days of strong Kōenkai
are also mostly over. If this is the case, then we should expect candidates
to run a more nationalized way and less on personal position.

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{H2}]: Candidates are increasingly campaigning on a national 
platform.
\end{itemize}
```

There are still some reasons to believe that this is not the case. The
above prediction has yet to be realized: the LDP won back in 2012 and
has remained in office since then. @catalinac18 does have empirical
evidence that shows that parties became more unified after the 1994
electoral reform.  The variance in within parties candidate positioning
reduces quite substantively after the electoral reform of 1994. While these
results are compelling, they stop at 2009 where the DPJ won the election.
As highlighted above by @reed_etal12, the LDP changed its campaign style
between 2005 and 2009 to a more nationalized one. Therefore, what we lack
now is how does the LDP responded *after* the electoral defeat of 2009.
Given that the less decentralized campaign appears to be associated with 
lower electoral results, and loss of power, for the LPD, it's important 
to see how did the party responded to this defeat. The fundamental question
is to understand if it went back to a more decentralized campaign, leaving
more discretion to its candidates. This could potentially explain why the 
party didn't loose another election after it won back in 2012.

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{H3}]: Within party candidates dispersion increases post-2009
\end{itemize}
```

## Model {#sec-model}

<!-- The previous model tries to answer this question by starting -->
<!-- from the assumption that party leader wants to win an election, and to -->
<!-- do so they have to maximize the total number of votes they receive in -->
<!-- each district. In this section, we will go over the previous explanations -->
<!-- that were proposed to answer this question, and see how do they compare -->
<!-- with the above model. -->

The setup goes as follows. A national party $P$ seeks to gain as many
votes as possible in order to win an election. To achieve this, it has
to convince the local population across the whole country to i) turn out
on the day of the election, and ii) vote for party $P$. To do this, the
party has resources that it can allocate across the different
constituencies to help promote certain candidates. The party $P$ also needs
to decide how *discretionary* its candidates can be in their campaign.
For simplicity, we will treat the allocation of resources as fixed for this
model, and focus exclusively on the *centralization* choice of party $P$.

The problem of centralization goes as follows. The leader ($L$) of
party $P$ does not know about the local needs and issues of all the
constituencies.  Therefore, by granting little discretionary power to
the candidates ($C$) running for its party, he runs the risk of alienating
part of the electorate. His priorities might be situated far from those
of the local population in constituency $d$.

On the other hand, the party leader can't delegate all the power and
discretionary choices to the candidates. Doing so would be
suboptimal, as his preferences might not be aligned with
those of all the candidates. Therefore, delegating all of his power to
the local candidates runs the risk of leaving these candidates to run on
"unwanted platforms". The party still wants to campaign on a relatively
similar platform. Therefore, the choice is to decide how far from the
party's national platform candidates can run.

The formalization goes as follows. In this game, we have one party leader
$L$ and $N$ candidates, one per constituency $d \in \{1, \dots, N\}$.
The party leader $L$ has utility preferences represented by
$u_L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\sum_{d=1}^{N} (x_d - \theta_d)^2$.
Here, $x_d$ represents the platform chosen by the candidate in
constituency $d$, and $\theta_d$ is the optimal point of constituency $d$.
Each constituency's optimal point is drawn i.i.d. from a distribution $F$,
$\theta_d \sim F$. The party leader doesn't observe the realization of
$\theta_d$, but he does know the distribution $F$.

The candidate in constituency $d$ has utility preferences represented by
$u_{C_d}(x_d, \theta_d, b) = -(x_d - \theta_d - b)^2$, where $x_d$ is
the candidate's platform, $\theta_d$ is the local optimal point, and $b$
is the bias, or disagreement, of the candidates with the party leader,
assumed common to all candidates.
Each candidate gets to observe $\theta_d$ before choosing their own 
platform $x_d$.

The game follows this timing: $L$ commits to a set of permitted platforms
$\mathcal{D}$; Nature draws $\theta_d$; candidate $d$ observes $\theta_d$;
candidate $d$ chooses $x_d \in \mathcal{D}$.

# Data

This project collects an original dataset using political bulletins in
Japan for the 2024, 2025, and 2026 lower house elections. The pipeline
goes as follow. We first developped a webscrapper to retrieve the election
bulletins from [go2senkyo.com](https://go2senkyo.com/).^[For the proposal,
I manually downloaded a samle of electoral bulletins from go2senkyo for
5 prefectures. For the final project, and for the continuation of this
project, I am working on a scrapper that will download the electoral
bulletin directly from the prefectures' electoral commission.] The website
compiles all the election bulletins across all districts retrieved from
each prefecture's electoral commission. The scrapper gets all the PDFs
files and store them locally. Once the files are downloaded, another
script uses Claude API to segment all the PDFs into the candidates running
inside district $d$. This approach is to facilitate the following step,
which is to use PDF parsing and OCR, and to increase the precision of
the information retrieved. About the parsing and the OCR, we used the
[Yomitoku](https://kotaro-kinoshita.github.io/yomitoku/en/) Python
librairy that is optimized for Japanese text and documents.

Once the parsing is done, we can store the information into a Pandas dataframe.
Each candidates (rows) have the following information attached to them: 
1) text from their election bulletin, 2) the number of paragraphs,
3) the number of headings, 4) the total number of characters (including both
Kanji and Kana).

The main challenge is to find an efficient way to extract the content 
from each bulletin per candidate. @fig-bulletin-ex shows an example of the 
structure of the PDF files containing all the candidates within a district.
Some tests made with Yomitoku on the complete pdf, like @fig-bulletin-ex, 
tend to introduce some parsing error. Some text was attributed to the wrong
candidates, images and layout tend to be more influential in the parsing 
potentially due to their relative size compared to the text, and some aspect 
of the layout tended to be overlooked by the parser. 

@fig-candidate-example present an example of an electoral bulletin for one 
candidate.
